title: Netanyahu Fights for Political Survival as Israelis Turn Out in Record Numbers for Historic Election
snippet: Israelis are heading to the polls at the fastest rate in over four decades, casting votes in a fiercely contested election that serves as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu's wartime leadership.
content:
JERUSALEM — Israelis cast their ballots in record numbers on Tuesday in a monumental election centered on the political fate of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the nation's path forward following the devastating Oct. 7, 2023 attacks.

With voter participation reaching its highest early turnout rate in 45 years—nearly 17% in the first three hours—citizens across the country are weighing Netanyahu’s aggressive wartime record against growing demands for accountability over the country's deadliest crisis in history.

A Nation Divided by War and Politics

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, faces a formidable challenge from former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. While Netanyahu touts his hawkish stance against regional adversaries and his close alliance with U.S. President Donald Trump, critics contend that his far-right coalition has deepened Israel’s international isolation and deepened domestic fractures.

Voters across the spectrum described the election as a critical turning point. "I think these elections are the most important of all the ones I’ve known," said Ruth Epstein, an 81-year-old voter from Ramat Gan who backed the opposition. "I’m really scared about what will be here."

Conversely, Netanyahu’s loyalists credited the prime minister for navigating complex geopolitical waters. Jerusalem resident Louis Lipsky pointed to the 2020 Abraham Accords, which normalized ties with several Arab nations, as reason to keep the veteran leader in power.

Eisenkot Pushes for Accountability and Reform

Eisenkot, leading a coalition spanning the center, right, and remaining left-leaning parties, focused his campaign on national healing and security reform. Visiting Kibbutz Nir Oz alongside released hostage Gadi Mozes, Eisenkot pledged to launch a formal national inquiry into the Oct. 7 security failures—a step Netanyahu’s government has consistently resisted.

"I am convinced that by the end of today, we will see a change — a new spirit for the State of Israel — that will serve as a rectification for the past three years and for that terrible day," Eisenkot told reporters.

Eisenkot has criticized Netanyahu's handling of the war in Gaza, arguing that failing to completely dismantle Hamas' governing apparatus represents a strategic error. He promised to eradicate Hamas' military capabilities within 18 months if elected, while also speaking out against West Bank settler violence that has strained Israel's alliances with Western nations.

Tight Race and Potential Gridlock

Netanyahu launched a late push to mobilize his base on election morning, calling on right-wing voters to hit the polls "en masse" to protect Likud's mandate. Far-right ally Itamar Ben-Gvir expressed confidence that Netanyahu would return to the helm with an reinforced conservative bloc.

Meanwhile, turnout among Israel's Arab citizens surged to high levels, potentially reshaping the parliamentary math. Arab coalition candidate Ahmed Tibi reported "unprecedented" turnout among Arab voters, who could play a pivotal role in preventing Netanyahu from securing a majority.

Political analysts predict a razor-thin margin. If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot can assemble a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker prime minister, setting the stage for continued political turbulence.
